opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think LEAP is really valuable, and the thing I like most about it is the "longitudinal" part. A lot of the discourse about AI timelines is people making one-off predictions, and then reality happens and nobody goes back to check who was right or how anyone updated. With a panel that's asked repeatedly over time, you can actually see how expert beliefs move as new capabilities come out. You can ask whether people were surprised, which way they were surprised, and whether the same people keep getting surprised in the same direction.

The second thing I find promising is that it pushes people to make concrete, resolvable forecasts. It's easy to say "AI will be transformative" or "it's all hype." It's much harder to say "here's my probability that a model hits this benchmark score by this date," or "here's what fraction of some kind of work I expect to be automated." Once you're forced into that format, disagreements become much more legible. Often two people who sound like they're in opposite camps turn out to disagree only about a factor of two on some timeline. Other times you find a genuinely deep crux, and that's really useful to surface.

I also like that it pulls from a fairly broad set of experts: computer scientists, economists, superforecasters, people in industry and policy. These communities often talk past each other. Economists tend to expect smoother, slower diffusion, and people close to the labs tend to expect sharper capability jumps. Putting them in the same structured exercise lets you see where those worldviews diverge and, over time, which one the evidence favors.

My caveat is that forecasting panels are only as good as the questions. If the questions are mostly about benchmarks, you can get a picture that's technically accurate but misses what matters, like whether AI systems can do long, open-ended, real-world tasks autonomously, or whether they're speeding up AI research itself. I think the most decision-relevant questions are about that kind of thing. So I'd love to see panels like LEAP keep moving toward measures that track real-world impact and autonomy, not just test scores. But as infrastructure for keeping ourselves honest about how fast things are moving, I think it's one of the better things out there.

r001.rationale: The response discusses granular forecasts and differences among expert communities, but does not explicitly link individual forecasts to forecasters’ longer-run worldviews.

r002.rationale: It praises repeated forecasts and checking them against outcomes, but does not suggest this is the most flexible tool available for tracking AI progress.

r003.rationale: The response does not discuss balancing early warning against making indicators credible enough to withstand skeptics’ criticism.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So the thing I find most promising about LEAP is pretty simple: it's longitudinal. We've had plenty of one-off surveys of AI researchers, and they're useful snapshots, but they're really hard to interpret over time because the sample changes, the question wording changes, and you can never tell whether a shift in the headline number reflects a real update or just a different crowd answering a different question. LEAP is trying to ask a fixed panel the same core questions repeatedly, so you can actually watch individual people's beliefs move and see what moved them.

The second thing is that it's not just asking "when will we get AGI." It's asking about a bunch of concrete, resolvable intermediate indicators, things like benchmark performance, revenue, automation of particular tasks, compute trends, and then pairing those with the longer-term, harder-to-resolve questions. That structure lets you do something I think is really valuable, which is check calibration on the near-term stuff. If a given forecaster, or a given cluster of forecasters, is consistently too bullish or too bearish on the things that resolve in six or twelve months, that tells you something about how much weight to put on their twenty-year views. Right now when experts disagree about timelines, there's basically no accountability mechanism. This creates one.

And relatedly, I like that it mixes populations. You've got AI researchers, you've got superforecasters, you've got people who work in the industry, and historically those groups have disagreed a lot, with the superforecasters tending to be more skeptical of fast progress. The interesting question isn't just who's right in the end, it's who updates appropriately as evidence comes in. If the superforecasters keep getting surprised on the upside by benchmark results and don't move their longer-term numbers, that's informative. If the AI researchers keep predicting capabilities that don't show up, that's informative too.

The honest caveat is that this only really pays off with time. The first wave of results is mostly a baseline. But I think building the infrastructure now, while things are moving fast, is exactly the right call. By the time it's obvious we needed this kind of data, it'll be too late to go back and collect it.

r001.rationale: The response connects repeated, granular predictions on resolvable indicators to longer-term views, saying near-term calibration can inform how much weight to give forecasters’ twenty-year views.

r002.rationale: It describes longitudinal forecasts and calibration as useful, but does not say that checking predictions against outcomes is the most flexible tool available for tracking AI progress.

r003.rationale: The response does not discuss balancing early warning with indicators being credible enough to withstand skeptics’ objections.

astra-6.text:
What I find promising is the longitudinal aspect: asking the same people questions over time, so you can see how their expectations change as new evidence comes in. With a one-off survey, if the answers differ from an earlier survey, it can be hard to tell whether people have updated or whether you’re just asking a different group of people.

I’d be interested in seeing where AI experts and people with strong forecasting track records disagree, and then following those disagreements. What developments cause them to update? Which expectations turn out to be more accurate? That could help us understand not just what people think is going to happen, but whose judgments are informative about which questions.

Of course, tracking expectations isn’t the same as measuring AI progress directly. You still need concrete outcomes to compare the forecasts against. But having a consistent record of what people expected, before they knew the answer, seems really valuable.

r002.rationale: It says forecasts should be compared with concrete outcomes, but does not characterize this approach as the most flexible tool for tracking AI progress; it explicitly distinguishes tracking expectations from measuring progress directly.

r003.rationale: The response does not discuss the tradeoff between indicators giving enough warning to act and being credible enough to withstand skeptics’ objections.

sol-6.1.text:
What I find promising is the longitudinal aspect: asking the same people questions over time, so you can see how their views change as new evidence comes in. If you just compare one survey of AI experts with another survey a few years later, it’s hard to know whether opinions have shifted or you’re simply asking different people.

And I think there’s a lot of value in making those expectations explicit ahead of time. What progress do people expect? Where do they disagree? What would surprise them? Then, as we observe what actually happens, we can start to understand which judgments were informative and where people’s intuitions were off.

I wouldn’t treat an expert panel as an oracle. But having a consistent record of people’s forecasts and updates seems much more useful than trying to reconstruct, after the fact, what everyone thought was going to happen.
